title: One of the biggest threats to working and leading better
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Muth Martinez names ambiguity as one of the biggest threats to working and leading well. She defines it through everyday workplace examples such as broad job descriptions, unclear decision rights, unexplained changes of direction, missing feedback channels and undefined metrics. Her claim is that ambiguity chips away at trust, exhausts people who must read between the lines, and is often used deliberately to dodge accountability and hoard power, particularly in under-resourced mission-driven organisations. She rebuts the view that vagueness is kindness or a way to avoid micromanagement by invoking Brene Brown's line that clear is kind. The piece closes with four reflective questions for leaders about where they create confusion and how to bring in clarity.
points: Ambiguity at work shows up as concrete, recognisable gaps: unclear roles, decision rights, direction, feedback and metrics.
It is not always accidental; it can function as a strategy to blur accountability and concentrate power.
Mission-driven organisations are especially prone because passion and commitment are used to cover for a lack of structure.
Leaders who think vagueness gives people space should treat clarity as care rather than control.
quotes: And while ambiguity can certainly be accidental, it’s often a strategy—used to dodge accountability, blur decision-making authority, and hoard knowledge and power. The more unclear the system, the easier it is to place blame and avoid responsibility.

It chips away at trust. People hesitate, second-guess, stall, overcompensate. They burn out trying to read between the lines—from all that emotional labor required to figure out what’s not being said.
But let’s remind ourselves of the fact that, per the lovely Brené Brown, “clear is kind.” Clarity isn’t control—it’s care. And ambiguity is the antithesis of care.

This isn’t just about language. It’s about culture. More specifically, how corporate culture uses sanitized, slippery language to dodge accountability while maintaining the illusion of productivity and professionalism. And over time, that illusion becomes a kind of gaslighting—a workplace reality distortion field that exhausts, demoralizes, and burns people out.

And especially in the context of mission-driven settings, where people are coming in with profoundly good intentions, going above and beyond—emotionally, intellectually, and physically—we owe them more than vague expectations and half-baked responses. We owe them the clarity that will actually help them fulfill the mission.
For the people doing the work, it’s demoralizing. For the organization, it can be utterly dismantling. But it’s sneaky.
